title: MTU shard truncate & eos-insert canary retro
body:
Summary:

On 2025-11-03 we observed a canary degradation in the eu-west-1 canary fleet that manifested as spuriously terminated responses (EOS tokens) for a subset of languages (es-419 and pt-BR). The canary was running a staged weight swap (quantized variant) for model v3.2.2 -> v3.2.3. An initial spike in 95/99th decode latency was followed by an increased error-rate in canaries and then a small but consistent increase in user-visible short responses (early EOS).

Short version: a network MTU mismatch between two relay subnets caused a partial truncation of a weight-shard transfer stream during the final stage of the canary weight apply. A truncated shard produced a mismatched parameter block that, when loaded by the quantized runtime, caused a rarely-triggered EOS-insertion decoding artifact for certain byte sequences in locale-specific tokenization. The issue only appeared in the canary cohort because the canary used microbatch reorder for throughput testing (different transfer timing) and a particular shard alignment that exposed the truncation boundary.

Detection / timeline (times UTC):
- 2025-11-03 01:12 — Canary rollout started (canary group alpha-eu-1) for model v3.2.3, rolling weight shards via streaming manifest apply.
- 2025-11-03 01:24 — Canary synthetic QA job (end-to-end decode tests) reports increased short-response rate for es-419.
- 2025-11-03 01:26 — First alerts: decode-failure-rate > threshold and canary p95 latency +120ms. Pager to eng-sre oncall.
- 2025-11-03 01:28 — SREs observe partial weight apply failures logged by the weight-apply consumer with I/O error: "read: unexpected EOF" on shard transfer stream.
- 2025-11-03 01:34 — Canary routing temporarily disabled for alpha-eu-1; rollback to v3.2.2 initiated.
- 2025-11-03 01:37 — Rollback completed; canaries stabilize and decode errors return to baseline.
- 2025-11-03 02:15 — Initial investigation finds asymmetric MTU configured on transit router between shard-store and canary relay subnets (1500 vs 9000).

Impact: 
- Canary cohort only (alpha-eu-1). No confirmed production user impact; route fallback and rollback prevented user traffic from hitting affected canary machines.
- Synthetic test suite showed 17% short-response rate for es-419 during the canary window (~01:24–01:34).
- Observability: temporary spike in weight-apply I/O errors (10 unique hosts) and per-shard checksum mismatches for two shard indices.

Root cause analysis (evidence):
1) Weight shard streaming uses a chunked transfer protocol with an expectation that underlying transport delivers ordered, untruncated byte streams. Logs show read errors with "unexpected EOF" during the final chunk for shard_0423 and shard_0424.
2) Network team confirmed a recent config change on the transit router (intended to limit jumbo frames in a legacy lane) set MTU to 1500 on the transit path from shard-store->relay. The canary relay hosts are on a path expecting 9000 (jumbo frames enabled) for large shard transfers.
3) The streaming transfer code did not have an explicit end-to-end per-shard byte-count verification at application layer; it relied on TCP retransmits and higher MTU assumptions. Retransmissions completed but a rare middlebox/driver interaction caused the last segment to be dropped and the socket closed by peer, producing the unexpected EOF observed.
4) The quantized model loader lacks a defensive check for full-blob length matching the expected parameter block size; when a truncated blob is loaded the runtime attempts to map the remaining bytes into quant metadata and padding, which in rare cases produced a degenerate attention bias vector that short-circuited token generation (early EOS) for byte sequences that align with locale-specific subtoken boundaries.
5) The microbatch reorder / canary throughput pattern caused a specific write-read interleaving on the two impacted hosts that exposed the transfer boundary (other hosts had successful transfers due to slightly different timing).

Mitigation & recovery steps performed: 
- Immediate: Canary routing disabled and automated rollback executed (by runbook) which replaced canary instances with previous model version and drained in-flight requests.
- Network rollback: network team reverted the transit router MTU to 9000 for the shard-store path to restore jumbo frames on that lane.
- Data integrity check: we re-ran per-shard checksums for all recently applied canary hosts; two hosts had truncated shards and were re-provisioned.
- QA: Synthetic end-to-end decode tests were run across locales (es-419, pt-BR, en-IN) to confirm no EOS bias after rollback.

Why this escaped prior checks: 
- No application-layer explicit length verification for shard blobs. Existing checksum verification runs after apply but the checksum routine assumes apply completes successfully; when a shard stream terminated early the apply step sometimes left a partial file and a checksum mismatch was logged but not elevated quickly enough.
- Network MTU changes are relatively rare and our deployment pipelines did not run pre-flight MTU validation for long streaming transfers.
- The quantized loader's data structures were not defensive against truncated metadata blocks (edge case but plausible).

Action items (owners + due dates):
1) Add application-layer per-shard byte-count validation and fail-fast on mismatch (owner: Liam Chen, due: 2025-11-17).
2) Enhance the weight-apply consumer to atomically write to temp file + verify checksum before moving into place; surfaced as high-priority alert on mismatch (owner: Priya Rao, due: 2025-11-14).
3) Add a network preflight check in rollout pipeline that verifies MTU and path MTU for shard-store routes (owner: Sofia Martinez + network team, due: 2025-11-10).
4) Harden quantized loader to validate parameter block size and metadata integrity with explicit error paths that abort load (owner: Model Runtime team, contact: Evan Brooks, due: 2025-11-21).
5) Add canary-level end-to-end locale decode smoke tests earlier in pipeline (pre-traffic) and make failure block rollout to further cohorts (owner: eng-sre + product-hosted-api, due: 2025-11-12).
6) Create alert that correlates weight-apply I/O errors + per-shard checksum mismatches and triggers immediate canary hold (owner: Observability team, due: 2025-11-09).
7) Postmortem blameless writeup and internal comms (owner: Aisha Patel, due: 2025-11-06).

Runbook updates (draft suggestions):
- Add explicit step after "streamed shard apply" to run 'verify-shard-bytes --expected-size <N> --path <file>' and abort if mismatch.
- If any read errors or "unexpected EOF" seen during apply, automatically mark host unhealthy and trigger re-provision + checksum reapply.
- Pipeline preflight to include a small MTU probe (tracepath/ping with DF) across shard-store->relay path and block rollout if mismatch detected.
- Add a canary gating rule: if synthetic decode short-response rate exceeds 5% for any locale, hold rollout and auto-run a limited checksum + network check.

Observability improvements: 
- Per-shard transfer duration histograms, and per-transfer bytes-sent vs expected-size metric.
- Instrument quantized loader to emit explicit "metadata-length-mismatch" metric and runtime abort counts.
- Dashboard: "Shard-transfer health" with node-level last-transfer-status, last-checksum, network-MTU at the time of transfer.

Open questions / follow-ups: 
- The exact middlebox/driver interaction causing the final segment drop is still under investigation by network infra. Need packet captures for the affected hosts (Liam to coordinate).
- Evaluate whether other streaming paths (model repo sync, large artifact distribution) have similar exposure.

Communication notes:
- Customer-facing: no action required; no confirmed user impact. Prepared short internal template for CS in case customers surface anomalies.
- Internal slack: concise incident summary posted to #sre-incidents and #infra-network (see linked_artifacts).

Appendix (quick debugging snippets):
- Grep pattern used to find failures: 'weight-apply.*unexpected EOF'
- Quick verify command: 'sha256sum <shard_file> && stat -c %s <shard_file> && cat <shard_file> | head -c 64 | xxd'

Notes to reviewers: this is written as a working retro. Prefer to discuss whether the preflight MTU probe should be in the deployment pipeline or as a separate network guard. Also want feedback on whether we should require atomic apply + checksum move for all artifact streams (safer but slows canary apply slightly).

Most immediate priorities for next 72 hours: 1) MTU preflight in pipeline (blocker), 2) weight-apply atomic move + checksum (high), 3) detect & auto-hold canary on decode short-response spike (high).

-- Aisha
